questions.q: Why do many research engineers check on running jobs before reading messages first thing in the morning?
options: It's a company policy at every lab
Compute is a shared, finite resource, and a silently failed run wastes an allocation the longer it goes unnoticed
Messages are always less important than any other task
Dashboards only update once per day
questions.explain: Catching an overnight failure early means it can be fixed and relaunched sooner, instead of wasting a shared GPU allocation for longer than necessary.

questions.q: Which sequence best matches the recurring rhythm described in this lesson?
options: Meetings, then lunch, then meetings again
Triage overnight runs, build or fix, launch and wait, discuss and write up
Write the paper first, then run the experiment
Only ever one task at a time with no context switching
questions.explain: The lesson describes a rough, often-revisited order: triage, build or fix, launch and wait, check in on long runs, and discuss and write up.

questions.q: How does this lesson characterize interruptions in a research engineer's day, compared to typical product engineering?
options: Interruptions are always harmful and should be eliminated
Interruptions are often the real work, not a disruption from it, because responding promptly protects expensive shared compute
Interruptions only happen during scheduled meetings
Research engineers never experience interruptions
questions.explain: Unlike the ideal of uninterrupted focus in much product engineering work, responding to a finished run or a flagged issue promptly is treated as central to the job.

questions.q: Why do research teams lean heavily on asynchronous communication such as written updates and dashboards?
options: Because synchronous meetings are banned at AI labs
Because a result might be ready at any hour, and the team needs to absorb it without everyone being online at once
Because asynchronous tools are cheaper than meeting software
Because research engineers dislike talking to each other
questions.explain: Since experiments finish on their own compute-driven timeline rather than a meeting schedule, async channels let results be absorbed whenever they land.

questions.q: What is meant by a "compute-paced day" in this lesson?
options: A day structured by how long experiments take to run rather than by a fixed meeting schedule
A day where no coding happens at all
A day measured strictly in 30-minute meeting blocks
A day where compute usage is billed hourly to each engineer
questions.explain: If a sweep takes six hours, the afternoon reorganizes around when those results land, which is why the day is paced by compute cycles more than the clock.
